questions.q: A client wants to run Orders/checkout. Where does it send the request?
options: Directly to the service on port 9080
To the Restate server's ingress on port 8080, which calls the service
To the admin API on port 9070
It publishes a message to a queue
questions.why: Clients always go through Restate. Restate records the invocation and pushes the work to the service.

questions.q: You changed a handler's code but Restate still seems to run the old version during development. What's the likely fix?
questions.why: Restate routes to registered deployments. Re-registering picks up the new handlers; Module 7 covers how production deploys new versions safely.

questions.q: Inside a handler, where should a call to a payment API go?
questions.why: Side effects go in ctx.run so they're journaled once. Outside ctx.run, they'd repeat on every replay.

questions.q: describe shows an invocation 'backing-off' with 'Connection refused' on the service URL. What's the most likely cause?
options: The service is down or unreachable
questions.why: Restate can't reach the service. Bring it back and the invocation resumes from its journal.

options: The email is sent before the next line runs
Once Restate accepts the send, the Emails handler will run, even if the caller crashes
Nothing; it's fire and forget with no guarantee
The caller receives the email's result
questions.why: Sends are durable: the caller doesn't wait, but delivery is guaranteed.

questions.q: A client sends the same request twice with the same idempotency-key header. What does Restate do with the second?
options: Attaches to or returns the result of the first invocation
Queues it to run after the first
questions.why: Restate deduplicates on the key (for a retention period, 1 day by default).

questions.q: A handler throws an ordinary Error because a supplier API returns 500. What does Restate do by default?
options: Retries with growing delays, eventually pausing if it keeps failing
questions.why: Anything that isn't a TerminalError is retried according to the retry policy; the default ends by pausing.

questions.q: An invocation is 'paused'. What should a support engineer suggest?
options: Delete it and ask the user to try again
Fix the cause shown in its last error, then `restate invocations resume`
Wait; it will retry on its own soon
questions.why: Paused invocations stop retrying and keep their journal. Once the cause is fixed, resume continues from where it stopped.

questions.q: A Reminders invocation is 'suspended' on a timer, and the service is shut down. What happens?
options: Restate reports errors until the service is back
Nothing until the timer fires; then Restate needs the service and retries if it's still down
questions.why: Suspended invocations don't need the service. Restate holds the timer.

questions.q: Two 'add' requests for Cart/dana arrive at the same moment. What happens?
options: They run at the same time and one change may be lost
They run one after the other; state can't be overwritten
questions.why: Exclusive handlers run one at a time per key. Different keys run in parallel.

questions.q: Which Restate feature fits 'a return approval that waits days for a human decision, once per return id'?
options: A workflow with a durable promise
questions.why: Workflows run once per key and can wait on durable promises that other handlers complete.

questions.q: A payment provider will call your webhook later with the result. How does a Restate handler wait for it?
options: Poll the provider every second inside ctx.run
Create an awakeable, give its id to the provider, await it; the webhook resolves it
Use ctx.sleep for an hour and hope
Store the order in a database and check it with a cron job
questions.why: Awakeables are durable callback tickets, completed via Restate's HTTP API or ctx.resolveAwakeable.

questions.q: In the saga, when do compensations run?
options: Only when a step fails with a TerminalError
questions.why: Transient errors are retried, not undone. Terminal errors trigger the catch block that runs compensations in reverse.

options: Not necessarily: check completion_result (success or failure)
No, completed means it was cancelled
questions.why: Completed means finished. Failed invocations are completed too, with completion_result = 'failure'.
